notes.b: Monosaccharides are the single-unit sugars, the simplest carbohydrates. Only some turn up in food as themselves, so it helps to know which foods supply each one.
points: Glucose occurs naturally in fruit, such as grapes, and in some vegetables, so everyday fruit and vegetables supply it.
Glucose syrup, a refined sugar used in sweets and processed foods, is another source of glucose in the diet.
Fructose, also called fruit sugar, occurs naturally in fruit and is the main sugar in honey. Honey contains both fructose and glucose, with fructose the larger part.
Galactose is not usually eaten free in food. It is released when lactose, the sugar in milk, is digested, which is why the marking schemes call it the sugar from digested milk.
Galactose comes from lactose, not from a plant food, so it is not a sugar you eat in quantity.
notes.tip: For a classification table, link glucose and fructose to fruit and honey, and galactose to digested milk. Do not give honey as table sugar.

notes.b: Disaccharides are double sugars, made of two sugar units joined together. Each common one has a typical food source, and much of the sugar in a modern diet is sucrose added to processed food.
points: Sucrose, the table sugar, is extracted from sugar beet and sugar cane and sold as white and brown sugar. It also occurs naturally in many fruit and vegetables.
Sucrose is added to biscuits, cakes, sweets, jam, fizzy drinks, breakfast cereals and other processed foods.

Lactose, the milk sugar, is found in milk and milk products such as yoghurt. If cheese is mentioned, only say that hard cheese has almost no lactose, because most of it is lost in the whey or fermented in making it; fresh and soft cheeses keep some.

Maltose, the malt sugar, is produced when starch is broken down during the germination of cereal grains, especially barley, which is the basis of malt. Malt is found in malted drinks, malt extract and malt loaf, and is used in brewing.
Added (free) sugars in processed food include those in biscuits, cakes, sweets, chocolate, jam, fizzy drinks, ice cream, breakfast cereals and sauces. Check the ingredients list to find them.
Natural sugars in whole fruit and vegetables and in milk come packaged with fibre and other nutrients. Added sugars supply energy with few other nutrients, which is why the two are not equal.
notes.tip: Match each sugar to its source: sucrose to sugar beet and cane (table sugar), lactose to milk, maltose to germinating barley. Maltose is not the sugar in table sugar, and honey is not table sugar.

notes.b: Starch is the main carbohydrate in the Irish diet and the main energy-supplying carbohydrate in staple foods (the basic foods a diet is built on). It comes mostly from cereals and from root crops.
points: Cereals and cereal products are rich in starch: bread, breakfast cereals, porridge oats, pasta, rice and flour. The grains themselves, such as wheat, oats, barley, maize and rice, are rich sources, and flour is made from ground grain.
Potatoes, rice, pasta and bread are the main starch foods in the Irish diet, so they are the easiest examples to give.
Potatoes and other root vegetables contain starch, and so do pulses such as peas, beans and lentils, which also contain fibre.
Porridge oats and many breakfast cereals are starch-based, so a breakfast of cereal or porridge is a starch source.
Glycogen, a polysaccharide, is present in small amounts in meat. It is not a significant dietary source.
notes.tip: When asked for one source of starch, give rice, pasta, potatoes, bread, flour or cereals. In a longer account, give about three sources for each class.

notes.b: Non-starch polysaccharides (NSP) are the plant polysaccharides, mainly cellulose and pectin, that human digestive enzymes cannot break down. Together they make up the dietary fibre of food, the part of plant food that passes through the gut undigested.
points: Cellulose is found in the skins of fruit and vegetables, in leafy and other vegetables, in wholegrain cereals and in bran. Wholemeal bread, brown rice, wholemeal pasta, nuts and seeds also contain it.

Pectin is found in the cell walls of fruit, especially apples and citrus fruit (the peel and pith of citrus). It is also in soft fruits such as gooseberries and blackcurrants, and unripe fruit has more.

Wholemeal and wholegrain products have more fibre than white versions because the bran, the outer layer of the grain, is kept. White flour and polished (white) rice have the bran removed in refining, so white bread has little fibre.
Seeds such as sunflower, sesame, pumpkin and linseed are high in fibre, as are nuts, and peas, beans and lentils.
Other good fibre sources are the skins of fruit and vegetables, fruit and vegetables generally, wholemeal bread, brown rice and pasta, bran, porridge oats and high-fibre breakfast cereals.
Fibre comes only from plants, so meat, fish, eggs and dairy foods contain none.
notes.tip: For three sources of fibre, choose from skins of fruit and vegetables, pulses, wholegrain products, nuts and seeds. Say wholemeal or wholegrain rather than just brown, and do not list fruit juice as a fibre source.

notes.b: Fibre sources fall into two kinds, depending on whether the fibre dissolves in water. This sorts the foods above into two groups.
points: Insoluble fibre is cellulose and wheat bran. Its sources are wholemeal bread, bran and vegetable skins.
Soluble fibre is pectin, plus the soluble fibre in oats, beans and lentils. Its sources are fruit, oats and pulses.

notes.h: Putting it together: foods by carbohydrate
notes.b: Exam questions often ask for sugar, starch and fibre sources side by side. A summary of foods by carbohydrate makes these easy to answer, and many foods contain more than one kind.
points: Sugars: fruit, honey, table sugar, sweets, jam, cakes, biscuits and milk. Starch: rice, pasta, potatoes, bread, flour and cereals. Fibre: wholegrain cereals, fruit and vegetable skins, nuts, seeds and brown rice.
Bread has starch, some sugar and fibre, with more fibre in wholemeal bread. Wholemeal bread should not be called high in sugar.
Fruit has sugars, pectin and cellulose, so it supplies a sugar and fibre together.
Potatoes in their skins have starch and fibre, while milk has lactose only.

Higher Level table: glucose, fructose and galactose come from fruit, honey and digested milk. Sucrose, lactose and maltose come from table sugar, milk and barley. Starch, cellulose and pectin come from potatoes and cereals, vegetables and fruit.
Poster or collage: head a poster with the classification groups (sugars, starch, fibre) and stick pictures of foods under each group.
notes.tip: If asked for one source each of sugar, starch and fibre, give a different food for each, such as table sugar, rice and wholegrain cereal. In a long account, give about three sources for each class.

keyTerms.definition: The disaccharide made of glucose and fructose, extracted from sugar beet and sugar cane as table sugar.
The disaccharide made of glucose and galactose, found in milk and milk products.
The disaccharide made of two glucose units, produced when starch breaks down during the germination of barley.
A polysaccharide that is the main carbohydrate in cereals, potatoes, rice and pasta.
A non-starch polysaccharide found in the cell walls of fruit, especially apples and citrus fruit.
A plant polysaccharide, such as cellulose or pectin, that the human digestive system cannot break down and that forms dietary fibre.
The outer layer of a cereal grain, rich in cellulose and removed when grain is refined into white flour.

questions.prompt: Name one dietary source of a monosaccharide, one of a disaccharide and one of a polysaccharide.
questions.model: Monosaccharide: glucose from fruit, or fructose from honey. Disaccharide: sucrose from table sugar, or lactose from milk. Polysaccharide: starch from potatoes, or cellulose from the skins of vegetables.

questions.prompt: Give an account of the dietary sources of sugars, starch and non-starch polysaccharides, and explain how choosing particular sources can improve the nutritional quality of the diet.
questions.model: Sugars: table sugar, honey, fruit, milk (lactose), and added sugars in biscuits, cakes, sweets, jam, fizzy drinks and cereals. Starch: potatoes, rice, pasta, bread, flour, breakfast cereals, porridge oats, peas, beans and lentils. Non-starch polysaccharides: skins of fruit and vegetables, wholegrain cereals, bran, seeds, nuts, pulses, apples and citrus fruit (pectin). Improvement: wholegrain bread, brown rice and pasta replace white versions to add fibre; fresh fruit replaces sugary snacks and juice; whole fruit and vegetables eaten with the skins on; naturally sugar-containing foods such as milk and fruit supply vitamins and minerals alongside their sugar.
